unit-az-latlong.title: Latitude and Longitude · Reading a Real Map
unit-az-latlong.srcName: The United States — US Bingo (Arizona Geographic Alliance)
unit-az-latlong.source: Built from the same US map used in class for latitude/longitude bingo — real cities, same 5-degree gridlines

summary.text: Practice reading latitude and longitude on the same United States map used in class for latitude/longitude bingo: the equator and Prime Meridian, why a coordinate needs both numbers, and — the main event — comparing and estimating real city positions using a 5-degree grid, without memorizing any one city's exact coordinate.

why.text: The skill that transfers is READING a grid — comparing positions, estimating between gridlines — not memorizing any one place's coordinate. Every question here is built to be answered from the map shown, not from a fact learned in advance.

objectives.text: Explain what a line of latitude and a line of longitude each measure, and from where.
Read a coordinate pair in the correct order.
Compare two or more real cities by latitude or longitude, and estimate a position between two gridlines, using the grid itself rather than a memorized fact.

parentNote.text: Rebuilt around the actual map from class (the Arizona Geographic Alliance US Bingo sheet, in her Drive folder) rather than an invented one — same 28 cities, same 5-degree gridlines from 130°W-70°W and 25°N-45°N (widened slightly here to fit a few cities right at the map's edge). On your note that flashcards shouldn't quiz exact coordinates for a place: every 'what is City X's coordinate' and 'which city is at this coordinate' question is gone, along with the cards that stated a city's coordinate as a fact to memorize. What is left is comparison (furthest north/south/east/west, ranking cities north-to-south or west-to-east) and estimation (reading a value between two gridlines, or judging which of several cities sits closest to a given line) — both answerable only by looking at the map in front of her, never by recalling a stored number. The country's outline is deliberately NOT drawn — a recognizable United States coastline is a much bigger shape than Arizona's near-rectangle, and a rough approximation of it risked looking wrong rather than helpful; the grid and the labeled cities carry the whole lesson without it.

nextUp.text: Run the cards once, then a quiz round with the map open.

unit-az-latlong.mapLabel: Map — see every city at once
unit-az-latlong.mapNote: The same 5-degree grid from class, with every city this unit asks about marked at once. Each question already shows its own slice of cities — open this any time you want to check one against the fuller picture instead.

cards.def:
**Lines that run east–west and measure distance north or south of the equator.**
• 0° at the equator, up to 90°N or 90°S at the poles.
• Every point on the same line of latitude is the same distance from the equator.
cards.hint: LAT-itude is FLAT-itude — the lines are flat, running side to side.

cards.def:
**Lines that run pole to pole and measure distance east or west of the Prime Meridian.**
• 0° at the Prime Meridian, up to 180°E or 180°W.
• Every point on the same line of longitude is the same distance around the globe from that meridian.
cards.hint: LONG-itude lines are LONG, running all the way from pole to pole.

cards.def:
**The 0° latitude line, halfway between the North and South Poles.**
• Everything north of it is the Northern Hemisphere.
• The whole United States sits north of it — every latitude on the class map is a °N.
cards.hint: The equator is a latitude line, so it splits the globe north-south.

cards.def:
**The 0° longitude line, running through Greenwich, England.**
• Everything west of it (up to the far side of the globe) is the Western Hemisphere.
• The whole United States sits west of it — every longitude on the class map is a °W.
cards.hint: The Prime Meridian is a longitude line, so it splits the globe east-west.

cards.def:
**Latitude is always given first, then longitude.**
• 33°N, 112°W means: find the 33°N line, then slide along it to 112°W.
• Swap the order and you would be looking for a completely different spot.
cards.hint: Alphabetical order helps: LAtitude before LOngitude.

cards.def:
**The same map from class — a 5-degree grid over the United States, with real cities marked.**
• Longitude lines run 130°W to 70°W.
• Latitude lines run 25°N to 45°N.
cards.hint: The lines are 5 degrees apart on this map — count gridlines, don't guess.

cards.def:
**A point does not have to land exactly on a line for you to read it.**
• If a point sits about halfway between the 30°N and 35°N lines, a good estimate is 32°N or 33°N.
• Being close is the goal — a map-reading estimate, not a measurement.
cards.hint: Which line is it closer to? Start there, then adjust a couple of degrees toward the other line.

cards.def:
**You can compare two places on a grid without ever reading off either one's exact coordinate.**
• The dot higher up the page is further north — true whether or not you read a single number.
• The dot further left is further west. Comparing positions is often faster than finding exact coordinates, and just as correct.
cards.hint: "Which one is further north" is a different, easier question than "what is its latitude."

cards.def:
**One coordinate alone only narrows you down to an entire line circling the globe.**
• Latitude alone: everywhere on that ring, the same distance from the equator — could be the US, could be Japan.
• Longitude alone: everywhere on that line, pole to pole. Together, the two numbers pin down one exact spot.
cards.hint: Think of it like a spreadsheet: the row number alone, or the column letter alone, isn't one cell — you need both.

questions.q: Lines of latitude measure how far a place is north or south of which line?
questions.hint: LAT-itude is FLAT-itude — think of the lines running side to side.
steps: Latitude lines run east-west, circling the globe like rings stacked from pole to pole.
Every ring is measured as a distance from ONE specific ring: the equator, at 0°.
So a latitude of 33°N means: 33 degrees north of that starting ring.

ex.main: **The equator.** It's latitude's zero line — every other line of latitude is measured as a distance north or south of it.
ex.tip: Latitude ↔ equator, longitude ↔ Prime Meridian. Keep the two pairs straight.

questions.q: Lines of longitude measure how far east or west a place is from which line?
questions.hint: LONG-itude lines run pole to pole, LONG ways around the globe.
steps: Longitude lines run pole to pole, like the segments of an orange.
Every segment is measured as a distance from ONE specific segment: the Prime Meridian, at 0°.
So a longitude of 90°W means: 90 degrees west of that starting line.

ex.main: **The Prime Meridian.** It's longitude's zero line, running through Greenwich, England — every other line of longitude is measured east or west of it.
ex.tip: Latitude ↔ equator, longitude ↔ Prime Meridian. Keep the two pairs straight.

questions.q: Based on latitude, which hemisphere is the whole United States in?
questions.hint: Every US latitude on the class map ends in N, not S.
steps: Every city on the class map carries an N after its latitude number, never an S.
N means north of the equator.
North of the equator is, by definition, the Northern Hemisphere.

ex.main: **Northern Hemisphere.** Every US latitude is a °N — the whole country sits well clear of the equator.
ex.tip: Hemisphere questions are usually just 'which letter does the number carry' in disguise.

questions.q: Based on longitude, which hemisphere is the whole United States in?
questions.hint: Every US longitude on the class map ends in W, not E.
steps: Every city on the class map carries a W after its longitude number, never an E.
W means west of the Prime Meridian.
West of the Prime Meridian is, by definition, the Western Hemisphere.

ex.main: **Western Hemisphere.** Every US longitude is a °W, and the whole country sits in the Western Hemisphere.
ex.tip: Hemisphere questions are usually just 'which letter does the number carry' in disguise.

questions.q: A coordinate is written 33°N, 112°W. Which number is the latitude?
questions.hint: One of the two labels is a hint about which kind of line it is.
steps: Latitude is always written first in a coordinate pair, by convention.
It also carries an N or S, since latitude counts north or south of the equator.
So in 33°N, 112°W, the 33°N is the latitude and the 112°W is the longitude.

ex.main: **33°N.** It comes first, and its N/S label is the giveaway — longitude always carries E or W instead.
ex.tip: Alphabetical order is the trick: LAtitude before LOngitude, same as in the alphabet.

questions.q: Which of these is written like a real US coordinate?
questions.hint: Check the order of the two numbers, and check both letters.
steps: Latitude comes first and never goes past 90° — so any option opening with 112° is already impossible for a latitude.
That rules out the option starting with 112°N.
Every real US coordinate carries N and W, never S or E — that rules out both remaining wrong options.
33°N, 112°W is the one in the right order with the right letters.

ex.main: **33°N, 112°W.** Order and hemisphere both have to be right — a coordinate that swaps either one points somewhere else on Earth entirely, or nowhere at all.
ex.tip: A latitude can never exceed 90° — that alone eliminates some wrong answers instantly.

questions.q: Two US cities share almost the same latitude, even though they're on opposite sides of the country. What does that tell you about them?
opts: They are about the same distance from the equator
They are about the same distance from the Prime Meridian
They must actually be the same city
One of the two coordinates has to be a mistake
questions.hint: Latitude measures distance from one specific line. Which line?
steps: Latitude measures distance north or south of the equator — nothing about east-west position.
Two cities can share a latitude while sitting far apart in longitude, like Boston and Detroit.
Sharing a latitude just means: same distance from the equator, wherever that lands east-west.
So same latitude, different longitude, is completely normal — not a mistake and not the same city.

ex.main: **They are about the same distance from the equator.** Latitude and longitude are independent — matching on one says nothing about the other.
ex.tip: Whenever two coordinates agree on one number but not the other, that tells you exactly one thing, not two.

questions.q: Using the map shown, which of these four cities is furthest NORTH?
questions.hint: Furthest north means the highest latitude — look for the dot nearest the top.
steps: Furthest north means the largest latitude number, so look for the highest dot on the map.
Denver, Atlanta and Miami all sit well below the 40°N line.
Seattle sits up near the top of the map, above the 45°N line.
Seattle is furthest north.

ex.main: **Seattle.** It's the highest dot on the map, up near the Canadian border — no gridline-reading needed once you see how far it sits above the other three.
ex.tip: 'Furthest north' always means compare latitude — the vertical position on the map — and ignore longitude entirely.

questions.q: Using the map shown, which of these four cities is furthest SOUTH?
questions.hint: Furthest south means the lowest latitude — look for the dot nearest the bottom.
steps: Furthest south means the smallest latitude number, so look for the lowest dot on the map.
Chicago sits highest of the four, well north of the others.
Dallas and Houston are both south of Chicago, but not as far down as the fourth city.
Miami sits lowest on the map, near the bottom edge — furthest south.

ex.main: **Miami.** It sits closest to the 25°N line, the lowest latitude of the four and the lowest dot on the map.
ex.tip: 'Furthest south' always means compare latitude, and smaller wins.

questions.q: Using the map shown, which of these four cities is furthest WEST?
questions.hint: Furthest west means the largest °W number — look for the dot nearest the map's left edge.
steps: Furthest west means the largest degrees-West number, so look for the dot nearest the map's left edge.
Boston sits close to the right edge, and Chicago and Denver are both well to the east of the fourth city.
Seattle sits close to the left edge of the map, near 122°W.
Seattle is furthest west.

ex.main: **Seattle.** At roughly 122°W, it's the largest degrees-West number of the four — and the leftmost dot on the map.
ex.tip: 'Furthest west' always means compare longitude — the horizontal position on the map — and ignore latitude entirely.

questions.q: Using the map shown, which of these four cities is furthest EAST?
questions.hint: Furthest east means the smallest °W number — look for the dot nearest the map's right edge.
steps: Furthest east means the smallest degrees-West number, so look for the dot nearest the map's right edge.
San Diego and Denver both sit well to the west, and Chicago is further east than either but still not the furthest.
Boston sits closest to the map's right edge, near 71°W.
Boston is furthest east.

ex.main: **Boston.** At roughly 71°W, it's the smallest degrees-West number of the four — and the rightmost dot on the map.
ex.tip: 'Furthest east' always means compare longitude, and smaller (closer to the Prime Meridian) wins.

questions.q: This one is closer than the others: using the map shown, which of these four cities is furthest NORTH?
questions.hint: Chicago and Boston are close on this axis. Which dot sits just a touch higher?
steps: Houston and Atlanta both sit south of the other two — that much is a clear read.
Chicago and Boston are much closer together, both hovering just under the 42°N line.
Looking carefully, Boston's dot sits a hair above Chicago's — a small gap, but a real one.
Boston is furthest north, though only barely.

ex.main: **Boston.** It's close — Boston and Chicago are only a fraction of a degree apart — which is exactly why this one is worth reading carefully instead of guessing from memory.
ex.tip: When two dots look almost level, that's the map telling you to look again, not to pick either one at random.

questions.q: Using the map shown, put these cities in order from FURTHEST NORTH to FURTHEST SOUTH.
questions.hint: Read straight down the map, highest dot first.
steps: Seattle sits at the very top of the map, well above every other city here.
Denver sits noticeably lower, but still north of the halfway point.
Memphis sits lower still, south of the 35°N line.
Miami sits at the very bottom of the map. Highest to lowest: Seattle, Denver, Memphis, Miami.

ex.main: **Seattle → Denver → Memphis → Miami.** Reading straight down the map from the highest dot to the lowest gives the same order as ranking the four latitudes from largest to smallest.
ex.tip: A north-to-south ranking is just a latitude ranking — ignore longitude completely.

questions.q: Using the map shown, put these cities in order from FURTHEST WEST to FURTHEST EAST.
questions.hint: Read straight across the map, leftmost dot first.
steps: San Francisco sits closest to the map's left edge.
Denver sits noticeably further right, closer to the middle.
Chicago sits further right still.
Boston sits closest to the map's right edge. Leftmost to rightmost: San Francisco, Denver, Chicago, Boston.

ex.main: **San Francisco → Denver → Chicago → Boston.** Reading straight across the map from the leftmost dot to the rightmost gives the same order as ranking the four longitudes from largest °W to smallest.
ex.tip: A west-to-east ranking is just a longitude ranking — ignore latitude completely.

questions.q: On the map shown, the latitude lines are 5 degrees apart. If a point sits exactly on the 35°N line and you move two gridlines north, what latitude are you at?
questions.hint: Each gridline is worth 5 degrees. North means the number goes up.
steps: This map's gridlines are spaced 5 degrees apart, since gy is set to 5.
Moving north means moving toward higher latitude numbers.
One gridline north of 35°N is 35 + 5 = 40°N.
Two gridlines north of 35°N is 40 + 5 = 45°N.

ex.main: **45°N.** Each gridline on this map is worth 5 degrees, so two lines north of 35°N adds 10 degrees.
ex.tip: Before answering a 'how many gridlines' question, check the grid's own spacing — it isn't always 1 degree.

questions.q: On the map shown, the longitude lines are 5 degrees apart. A point sits exactly on the 100°W line. If you move one gridline east, what longitude are you at?
questions.hint: Each gridline is worth 5 degrees. East means the °W number goes down.
steps: This map's gridlines are spaced 5 degrees apart, since gx is set to 5.
Moving east means moving toward smaller degrees-West numbers, not larger ones.
One gridline east of 100°W is 100 − 5 = 95°W.
105°W would be one gridline WEST instead, and 100°E confuses this map's own hemisphere entirely.

ex.main: **95°W.** Moving east always shrinks the degrees-West number on a US map — the opposite direction adds to it.
ex.tip: Before answering, decide which way the numbers move for the direction you're asked about — it's easy to reverse by accident.

questions.q: Using the map shown, which of these four cities sits closest to the 40°N gridline?
questions.hint: Find the 40°N line, then see which dot it almost passes through.
steps: Find the 40°N gridline on the map — it runs between Chicago's row and Denver's row.
Chicago sits a little above it; Atlanta and Miami both sit well below it.
Denver sits just barely below the line — the closest of the four to actually touching it.
Denver is closest to the 40°N gridline.

ex.main: **Denver.** Its dot sits nearly on the 40°N line itself, closer than any of the other three.
ex.tip: "Closest to a gridline" is a distance comparison, same as "furthest north" — just measured against a line instead of against each other.

questions.q: Using the map shown, which of these four cities sits closest to the 90°W gridline?
questions.hint: Find the 90°W line, then see which dot sits right beside it.
steps: Find the 90°W gridline on the map, near the map's middle.
Atlanta and Boston both sit well to the east of it, and Chicago sits a couple of degrees east too.
Memphis sits right beside the 90°W line, closer than any of the other three.
Memphis is closest to the 90°W gridline.

ex.main: **Memphis.** Its dot sits almost directly on the 90°W line, closer than Chicago, Atlanta, or Boston.
ex.tip: When two cities look close together, check them both against the actual gridline rather than against each other.
